voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudFoot.holeOverSeatPro: READ off the 2010 deck plate (Wikimedia Commons, 'Hokulea deck and sleeping area.JPG', 4000 × 2672 px; r265/crop-deck-2-x1700.png and crop-deck-3-x2550.png, the plate's x 1700–3550 and y 1000–1700 at 1.5x). The hole's centre stands 505 ± 20 px at 1.5x — 337 px on the plate — over the top of the wrapped timber: 0.42 m ± 0.10 vertically, 0.45 m along the shroud's 20° lean, which is what the model's lash sets. The TWO FARTHER feet (plate x 3000–3300, about 3.6 times the nearest heart's distance, their hearts 80 px long) hang with their holes roughly 0.75 m over the waist-high rail below them and their lanyards run more than a metre down behind the rail's canvas before the plate loses them, so those two stand higher over their timber than the nearest one and by an unread amount; a lanyard's length is whatever the shroud's made length leaves, so the height need not be one figure for every foot. The record carries the nearest foot's read as the height for every foot; which feet stand higher is not readable (which beam each shroud takes, 0y⁴⁵, is not either). Before round 266 the model's height was the class figure 0.3 B (0.315 m), and round 265's read of the nearest hole 0.09 m over 'the cap rail' was a projection — that rail stands behind the heart at 3.6 times its distance, so a like height reads lower on the plate. Round 266.
voyaging-canoe.hull.masts[0].shroudFoot.provenance: READ off the Marine Education Training Center series of 18 May 2010 (Wikimedia Commons, 'Hokulea deck and sleeping area.JPG', 4000 × 2672 px, CC BY-SA 3.0, Hōkūleʻa moored at Honolulu Community College with her crew off, the near hull's rail seen from the pier between the masts; r265/metc-2010-deck-sleeping.jpg, crops r265/crop-deck-*.png at 1.5x and crop-bullseye-3x.png), with the same fitting at every foot in 'front with masts', 'front and sleeping area', 'head on' and 'stern from side' of the same series (r265/metc-2010-*.jpg). The scale is the shroud's own rope: 20 px thick on the nearest heart (plate x 2300–2700, y 1050–1450), taken as a one-inch three-strand line, 25 ± 5 mm, so 800 ± 160 px/m there; the heart is 290 px long and 177 wide, 0.36 × 0.22 m ± 0.07, its lower tip about 0.14 m below the cap rail's top and its hole 0.09 m over it on that foot, the pair at plate x 3000–3300 standing about 0.3 m clear of the cap; its thickness is unread (the plates are face-on) and the model's 0.05 m is a class figure. Which beam each shroud takes is NOT read from these plates: the deck plate is a perspective along the rail from abeam of the fore mast and the bow-quarter plates foreshorten the rail, so a foot's station cannot be placed against a beam's without a scaled plan (0y⁴⁵ stands). The 2019 plate 'Hōkūleʻa mast.jpg' (Commons, 4608 px) shows WIRE shrouds converging at the head on a metal fitting: that is the rig after the 2012–13 dry-docking for the worldwide voyage, not the 2009 rig the model draws. Before round 265 the lashing class ended every shroud in a rope eye 0.3 B over the beam, a class figure read from no plate. Round 265.

trireme.hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r179 — the windlass question for this hull, the last of the r172 line, closes with nothing drawn, and on a third shape of silence: not r176's inference stack over a later-era machine, not r178's tradition with nothing to extend, but a complete inventory that omits the machine. The Athenian navy kept stone-cut inventories of its dockyards — the fullest gear record of any ancient ship class — and the lists of entire equipment (entele skeue) supplied to three- and four-banked ships from 330/329 BC enumerate everything aboard: two iron anchors per warship (CIA II 807/808/809/811, 'ankyras sideras dyo' in every case), eight cables in two recorded sizes, four for the bow anchors and four shore-cables (epigya) that moored her stern to the beach (Torr, Ancient Ships 1894, notes 161 and 166, the inscriptions quoted verbatim), the hypozomata among the hanging gear, oars, rudders, ladders, poles, masts, yards, sails, screens — and no windlass, winch or capstan anywhere. The inventory even weighs the anchors: CIA II 807 col. b (329 BC) records iron anchors at a stated weight of twenty-odd mnas — under half a hundredweight in Torr's reading of the damaged numeral, named as his. Torr's whole book, downloaded in r177 and grepped again this round, has one windlass sentence (p. 95), and it is the sail-tackle of the big Roman merchantmen — the corbita's own r177 evidence. The Greek word for the shipboard machine, stropheion, boards a ship exactly once in the record, on Lucian's Isis (Nav. 5, c. AD 165, the corbita's r177 warrant, six centuries after this hull's drawn year); its classical-era epigraphic use is the Delian harbour accounts (IG XI(2).138 B 8, iv/iii BC; LSJ s.v.), where stropheia are dues ships paid for the USE of a windlass — the machine stood on the quay. And Herodotus' own word for it, onos, appears in this hull's own drawn year: the Hellespont bridge cables of 480 BC, laid over pontoon triremes, were made taut from the land — ek ges — with wooden windlasses, onoisi xylinoisi (Hdt. 7.36.3, fetched verbatim in Greek and English; LSJ's other windlass citations are a bone-setting frame and the Mechanics, none shipboard). Her world knew the machine; its place was the shore, and aboard her it had no work: anchors of under ~25 kg, some 200 hands, a 47 t hull moored stern-to with her own listed shore-cables and hauled out on the ship-sheds' slipways — she was the thing the shore's machines and men hauled. r177 drew the corbita's windlass because her ship's own gear list names one; this hull's own gear lists, far fuller than Lucian's sentence, omit it — the same class of source, obeyed both ways. Stated: the entire-gear lists are the 4th-century navy's, some 150 years after the drawn year (-480); they are the class's fullest record at any date and the 5th-century evidence points the same way, but the gap is named. Scope: the judgment is for the classical trireme as her navy inventoried her; the giant polyremes of the Hellenistic age are different ships, and their gear (Moschion's forty carried twelve anchors) is not read backward here. That the crew worked anchors and hypozomata by direct pull is an inference, marked as one on the card. Named as not fetched: Morrison, Coates & Rankov's The Athenian Trireme and Rankov's Olympias Final Report (both gated; both already this card's cited hull sources), and the IG II2 stones beyond Torr's transcriptions (PHI search script-gated, Attic Inscriptions Online HTTP 500 for IG II2 1604) — any of them, fetched and attesting a shipboard winding machine on a trireme, reopens the question.

corbita.hull.steeringProvenance: Roman seagoing ships steer with a pair of great quarter rudders — the Sidon and Portus reliefs and the Ostia mosaics draw them, and no Roman wreck or image shows a sternpost rudder (Casson, Ships and Seamanship in the Ancient World). DERIVED in size from the hull; the reliefs are profile carvings with no usable scale.
corbita.hull.windlassProvenance: The gear list of her own trade's giant, thirty-five years before her drawn year. Lucian, Navigium 5 (c. AD 165), on the Alexandrian grain freighter Isis at Piraeus — the ship this card's own rows carry: 'αἱ ἄγκυραι καὶ στροφεῖα καὶ περιαγωγεῖς καὶ αἱ κατὰ τὴν πρύμναν οἰκήσεις, θαυμάσια πάντα μοι ἔδοξε' — the anchors, the windlasses and the capstans, and the stern cabins, all of them wonders to the visitor. Torr (Ancient Ships, 1894, p. 95) and the fetched translation read the two nouns as the ship's winding machines; which noun is the horizontal machine the text does not say, and ONLY the horizontal windlass is drawn — a Roman vertical winch has no attested form, and the Georgian capstan this hull carried until r172 was exactly that anachronism, removed. Lucretius 4.901–906 puts the machina with its trocleae and tympana — pulleys and drums moving great weights at light effort — in the same breath as the ship and her rudder; Torr's note connects the Latin terms to Lucian's Greek ones, a scholarly reading named as such. Warrant: GEAR-LIST EXTENSION, same trade, same era — one stated inference, from the 55 m Isis down the same Alexandria–Rome run to the drawn 40 m carrier (the Madrague de Giens size, the card's other named wreck). Station u 0.15 is a PLACEMENT INFERENCE ±0.05: no ancient source places the machine; the bower anchors and their cables work at the bow — hawse-eyes and catheads a little abaft them (Torr pp. 69–74) — and the drawn station is the open foredeck abaft the artemon's step. Barrel 3.6 m is a GEOMETRIC read off the drawn deck's breadth at that station (probe, read-only, before this record was written); diameter 0.5 m, the axis a foot over the deck and the two standards are Falconer CLASS DEFAULTS cross-tradition (r173). CONTESTED, the standing negative: Laurons 2, the one wreck preserved to the rail (late 3rd c. AD, a ~15 m, ~30 t coaster), keeps her bitts, belaying pins and spare rudder and shows NO windlass in any fetched description — the class's small end may have worked its anchors by hand, and a corbita drawn at her size would reopen this judgment toward silence. No fetched relief or mosaic shows the machine; Casson 1971 is borrow-gated and was not readable this round, named as such.

dhow.hull.grapnelProvenance: DRAWN, r182 — the head of the anchors line, on the strongest warrant any ground tackle in this fleet carries: the drawn instance's own wreck preserved the anchor. Flecker's excavation report names it — 'the ship's nautical equipment may be represented by a composite grapnel-type anchor, the shank of wood and the arms of iron' (World Archaeology 32:3, 2001; the hedge is the author's) — and the excavation monograph gives the form: the arms protrude straight outward and are separated vertically by a heavy bell-shaped iron disk with a hole through the centre, the disk a shape that lends itself to casting, the arms thought to be wrought iron; only the lower end of the wooden shank survived, and one arm is broken (Flecker in Krahl, Guy, Wilson & Raby, Shipwrecked: Tang Treasures and Monsoon Winds, Smithsonian 2010, pp. 112–13, figs. 84–85, fetched whole this round). DIMENSIONS are the plate's own: fig. 84 carries a 100 cm scale bar, read at 2.5 px/cm in a 300-dpi render — the intact arm pair 1.72 m tip to tip (plan and both elevations agree within 4 mm of drawing), the crossing pair 1.44 m as drawn with its broken arm, arm shafts ~0.12 m as drawn (concretion not separable; the model draws 0.10 m), the bell ~0.55 m across the base and ~0.13 m high, the shank stub ~0.16–0.20 m thick, its foot protruding below the bell. The broken pair is drawn complete at the intact pair's span (inference). The SHANK'S LENGTH is preserved nowhere: 1.8 m is a reconstruction — about the arm span over again, shank enough for the crown to trip and the head to take the cable clear of the arms — and no fetched source preserves or reconstructs it. Shank timber Afzelia sp. or Amoora sp. (CSIRO identification, Flecker 2001); the bell may be Chinese-cast — cast iron was China's alone in the 9th century — and the tradition's own navigational literature names an iron grapnel al-hadid, 'the iron', and an anchor type al-anjar al-siniya, 'the Chinese anchor' (Ibn Majid, via Flecker 2010). STOW: loose on deck at the bow — the tradition's documented practice at its recorded end (Lockerbie, catnaps.org, r178's fetch: Gulf craft stow the anchor loose on deck or hang it on the kalba at the prow), and the Maqamat images hang the four-pronged grapnel at the prow (Agius, Classic Ships of Islam, 2008, ill. 32, form only, no scale readable). That a 9th-century crew stowed it the same way is an inference between those attestations; station u 0.125 — the open foredeck between the stem and the foremast's step — and the stow attitude (the shank laid aft and yawed to pass the mast's foot, measured against the drawn deck) are PLACEMENT INFERENCE: no source places the anchor aboard. Named as not fetched: the Jewel of Muscat replica's build record (jewelofmuscat.tv unreachable this round, HTTP 404 on every tried path) and Vosmer's PSAS paper (pay-gated, r178) — either, fetched and giving a reconstructed shank, would replace the stated 1.8 m.
dhow.hull.windlassProvenance: JUDGED SILENT, r178 — the windlass question for this hull, opened by the r172 residual, closes with nothing drawn, and this field says why. The drawn ship is the sewn early type (this record's own steering provenance), the Belitung wreck's tradition, and the evidence is silent at every documented point of that tradition. Her own wreck's excavation report, read whole this round, mentions no windlass, winch or capstan anywhere; the ship's nautical equipment 'may be represented by a composite grapnel-type anchor, the shank of wood and the arms of iron' (Flecker, World Archaeology 32:3, 2001) — though the wreck preserves the lower hull only, so its machine silence is weak and is not leaned on. What decides is the tradition itself: Agius's Classic Ships of Islam (Brill 2008), the scholarly survey of this ocean's ships from the 7th to the 16th century, read whole this round, describes the anchors of every period — Omani stone anchors with sharp-ended timbers fitted through, Indo-Arabian stone shanks at Siraf (8th–11th c.), Ibn Sida's wood-and-lead anchor recipe (d. 1066), Correia's iron-and-stone and Varthema's marble anchors (16th c.) — each topped by a hawser hole and a rope, and names no winding machine in gear, crew roles or terminology anywhere in the book. At the tradition's best-documented end, the Gulf craft of the last working-sail century stow the anchor loose on deck or hang it on the kalba cat beam at the prow, take lines to bitts and the rumaana bollard, and acquire a winch only 'with the advent of power' (Lockerbie, catnaps.org, fetched whole). Unlike the junk (two primary texts), the panokseon (the living horong) and the corbita (her own trade's gear list), this tradition attests no machine at any era to extend from — drawing one would invent existence, form and place at once, the class of error the r172 Georgian capstan was. The record stays silent and the builder draws nothing. That her crew worked the grapnel by direct pull is itself an inference, marked as one on the card. Named as not fetched: Villiers' Sons of Sinbad (borrow-gated, search-inside blocked too), Vosmer's reconstruction chapter (403), the PSAS Jewel of Muscat paper (pay-gated), Agius's two other dhow books — any of them, fetched and attesting a sail-era machine, reopens the question. Scope: the judgment is for the drawn sewn trader and the sail tradition as documented; a powered conversion's winch is a different ship.

junk.hull.windlassProvenance: The bow machine of her own tradition, eyewitness-attested at her own size and century. Xu Jing, Gaoli tujing (1124), ch. 34, on the Song sea ships (kezhou, ten-odd zhang): 'between the two cheek-posts at the ship's head there is a winch wheel, on which is wound a rattan cable as thick as a rafter, five hundred feet long; below hangs the anchor stone, two wooden flukes clamped at its sides ... getting under way, they roll the wheel up and recover it.' The Tiangong Kaiwu (1637) confirms the arrangement as standing practice: the yun che windlass winds the cable to raise the iron anchors, belayed to the two 'general's posts' at the brow of the bow. Station u 0.10 is a TEXT read (at the head, between the posts), +/-0.04 u — no plate, no plate scale. NO barrel dimension survives in either text: length 4.6 m is a GEOMETRIC class default (the barrel spans the foredeck between the posts; the drawn deck is 6.63 m wide at the drawn station, the audit's own measure), diameter 0.5 m and the 0.30 m underside height are CLASS DEFAULTS (Falconer 1769 cross-tradition, as r173's cog), post height 1.6 m a CLASS DEFAULT (the posts belay the cable, so they rise past the barrel). Needham IV.3 and Worcester were NOT fetched (access-restricted scans); this record cites the primaries directly.
junk.hull.stoneAnchorProvenance: RECORDED, r199 (form and dimensions), on the r183 eyewitness warrant — the windlass's own load, from the same sentence that drew the machine (Xu Jing, Gaoli tujing 1124, ch. 34, warrant DIRECT: his kezhou is this hull's own size, class and century): 'below hangs the anchor-stone; on the stone's two sides it is clamped by two wooden hooks' (下垂矴石，石兩旁，夾以二木鈎), on a rattan cable thick as a rafter, no iron anywhere. THE FORM IS THE EXCAVATED ONE since r199: the two-shank stone-insert anchor (두 개의 닻채 사이에 닻돌을 끼어 넣고) of the 2017 마도해역 시굴조사 보고서 (국립해양문화재연구소, fetched and mined r198) — two cheek timbers pegged with cross battens, each sweeping outward to a curved fluke point, the stone wedged crosswise through the gap between their seat faces, its ends projecting both sides as the stock, forcing the fluke plane vertical on the bottom. The report itself reads the type as CHINESE practice — 마도해역-203 came up with one arm and a braided bamboo cable, the cordage it names Chinese, its stated analogue the anchor on the Eastern-Han pottery ship excavated at Dongjiao, Guangzhou, 1951 — and the Mado anchorage sits on the Goryeo west-coast sea road Xu Jing's own fleet sailed in 1123. The text's clause lands on the artifact exactly: the stone's two broad faces are what the two hook-timbers clamp, 石兩旁. A second stone records that grip in its own dressing (read r200, page verified by eye r201): 진도-621, the one Chinese-form stone at Myeongnyang (보고서 Ⅰ 2015, p. 447; report Ⅲ's synthesis names it direct evidence of a Chinese ship in the strait) — 175.6 × 22.8 × 13.2 cm, 108 kg, bar-form, symmetric, finely dressed, a 13 cm seat groove cut on BOTH broad faces (내외면) where the 닻채 timbers seat and ~4 cm grooves top and bottom for retaining pins (고정못) — the third measured insert stone after 203/206/212, and the first with the seat itself dimensioned. THE DRAWN OBJECT IS 마도해역-212 AT ITS OWN SIZE, the one find in the tradition where arm and stone survive as one object (raised 2014-08-01 still articulated, 결구된 채 — the report states this proves the insert structure). Stone: the report's printed record, 109 × 29 × 10 cm, 84 kg. Arm: no printed dimension exists, so the timber is MEASURED off the report's own 1/10 catalogue drawing (p. 210, rendered at 300 DPI, 4.06 px/cm against its printed 50 cm bar — the plate reproduces the stone's printed 29 cm width to 0.1 cm at the same scale, and the arm agrees across its three views to 0.3%): run 1.49 m tip to butt, section 0.16 × 0.15 m, the fluke sweeping 0.285 m off-axis over the outer 0.81 m and tapering to a ~0.07 m point, the stone seat a shallow 0.25 m waist cut 1.02–1.27 m from the tip (the plan's stone crossing reads 1.02–1.29 — joinery and plan agree, drawn at seat centre 1.15), three square mortises at 0.58, 0.90 and 1.37 m carrying the battens — Hong 2013's artifact ⑤, 'the Mado arm with three square holes', by its own excavation record. Assembly per the report's complete-form schematic (완형 추정 모식도, p. 205): seat faces inward the stone's thickness apart, the cable bent round the mid batten and led out between the horns. SCALE IS CONTESTED: 84 kg reads as a coastal trader's anchor, and the kezhou's great anchor — a four-man windlass, a 500-chi cable — likely swung heavier; the corpus's measured ceiling is 마도해역-203 (98 × 40 × 34 cm, 255 kg; = the 2023 닻돌 report's stone 052) with 마도해역-206 between (178 × 28 × 13 cm, 133 kg, an 18 cm 결구부 seat and retaining grooves cut mid-length). But no larger pair survives measured, a scaled-up 212 would be a derivation with an invented factor, and the record beats a derivation from the record — the smaller true object over the larger invented one, the gap stated here. The cable's 0.10 m diameter stays an INFERENCE from the text's simile (其大如椽), its 500-chi length the record's, not drawn whole. STOW is PLACEMENT INFERENCE: under way the anchor rides recovered (收之) on the open foredeck between the stem and its own windlass, head aft, cable to the barrel (上綰藤索); the assembly is cruciform in section — horns on one axis, the stone crossing the other — so it cannot lie flat, and it is drawn at repose, rolled onto one stone end and one horn, settled to the deck by measurement. The r183 hang finding stands: a hung anchor sits pocketed out of every broadside view behind this hull's bluff bow shell (raycast, r183), so a hang would be invisible and is not drawn. The text's two spare roving anchors (游矴) are NOT drawn: attested in use only, no stow named — drawing one would invent place. CORROBORATED IN PRINT, r203: the 송호리1호선 excavation report (해남, 국립해양유산연구소 2025; fetched whole from the institute's board, 35,320,352 bytes byte-exact) catalogues the form's one aboard-ship record in anything fetched here — one oak timber cut as 닻채 and 닻가지 together (the analysis report's species table reads its sample 42, named 닻가지, 상수리나무류), made to be joined face-to-face with an identical opposite half, printed at 최대길이 149.5 cm, 최대 폭 91.3, 최대두께 19.1 cm, 28 kg (p. 160, plate read by eye), with three through-stations in the shank and a 'ㄷ'-section groove between the lower two that the report reads as the stone's joint (닻돌 결합부(추정)) — found INSIDE the hull, port side near the stern, and the hull's own plank is radiocarbon-dated AD 1021–1158 (Beta Analytic 2σ; CAL 1040–1220; the dendro study fells the bark-bearing bottom plank at 1055–1085): Xu Jing's own century, on the same west-coast road at its Haenam turn. The printed 149.5 cm stands half a centimetre from the 1.49 m this record measures off 212's drawing, and the photographs show the three stations as square mortises — 212's own joint detail. Contested within that report and named here: its survey chapter calls the stations 나무못 구멍 (peg holes), its catalogue 관통 구멍 bound 줄로 (rope through-holes); 212's own halves are pegged with cross battens. And the carrier is a Korean-built 전통 한선 coaster, so the 2017 report's Chinese-practice reading widens — the form served both hull traditions on this coast — without unseating its cordage and analogue evidence. The ship's three catalogued 닻돌 (9.2, 151.3, 8.3 kg) are all grooved lashed-form; none is an insert-seat stone, and the anchor's own stone is not identified among them. The 151.3 kg stone's rock is contested between the site's own two reports — 역암 by the excavation catalogue, 화산력응회암 by the analysis report's petrology, which also prints different dimensions (133.6 × 55.8 × 16.7 cm vs 1,335 × 593 × 226 mm) — both stated.

treasure-ship.hull.ironAnchorProvenance: DRAWN, r184 — a FLEET-CLASS EXTENSION, the same join as the windlass: this hull's own record attests no fitting (attestation 'generated'). The Tiangong Kaiwu (1637, ~200 years after the voyages — the gap named) carries the object in two chapters. Zhouche counts the inventory for the state grain ship: five or six iron anchors, the mightiest the kanjia mao (sheet anchor) at about 500 catties RECORDED, two worked at the head, two at the stern, cables belayed to the two general’s-posts and broken out by the yun-che windlass; and ‘the ocean transport’s gear is all the same’ (qi ju jie tong) carries the set to the zheyang ship, the Yuan and early-Ming state sea carrier (the r174 join, build/staging/r174/JUDGMENT.md). NO dimension is in any text; a measured surviving four-claw anchor now sets the scale (r188 — the replacement this field promised). 蓬莱水城出土 1984 — the complete excavated Ming four-claw anchor from the Penglai naval fortress, 全長 2.15 m at 456 kg (Matsui 2013 fig. 3 caption, after 王冠倬 2000: 149, 277–278; the paper local since r187, its fig. 3 read on the plate r188) — calibrates weight to length by cube-law within the one tradition: the 500-catty (~295 kg) sheet lands at 1.86 m full length; the pair’s 300 catties — still an INFERENCE at the forging text’s own anvil threshold, the text records only the sheet’s weight — at 1.57 m, carried to the stern pair whose weight is not recorded. The record fields carry the FULL crown-to-ring length a find’s 全長 measures (the r187 yotsume convention; the drawn ring top lands at the field’s value). Cross-check: 泉州四湖港出土 1981, 残高 2.68 m at 758.3 kg — incomplete, its missing parts dotted in the figure, weighing less than the ~880 kg cube-law gives a complete 2.68 m: a consistent lower bound. Sensitivity NAMED: fig. 3b, 山東省梁山県宋金河出土 1956, 全長 1.36 m, the shank inscribed 「甲字五百六十号 八十五斤 洪武五年」 — an as-made 85 catties (~50 kg) in 1372, the corpus’s slender small-craft build at less than half Penglai’s weight per length; a power law through both dated Ming points would give 1.96 m sheet (inside the audit’s 12% band) and 1.77 m pair (at the band’s edge). Penglai — the naval-fortress find of the state build the forging text describes — is the calibrator for a state ship’s tackle; the choice moves the drawn anchor by a hand’s width and is recorded here. Claw sweep MEASURED r189, from the calibrator's own drawing — fig. 3a self-scales, 全長 2.15 m in its caption; the plate read at 322.8 px/m from a 300-DPI render (build/staging/r189). The drawing is 王冠倬's published line drawing of a corroded find, so the proportions carry its draughting precision, not a survey's. The pair drawn widest is read as in-plane; the two sides give reach 0.325/0.354 of 全長 and tip height 0.222/0.181 — the spread is the obliquity bound — and the means set the class: tips at 0.339 of 全長 from the shank axis, 0.201 above the crown centre, the arm leaving the shank foot near-flat and turning up to ~40° at the point, arm sections tapering 0.024 → 0.009 of 全長, the head a small forged eye 0.062 across in place of the drawn wide ring, the crown ball 0.078 — its bottom, the datum 全長 measures from, 0.039 below the claw joins. The audit holds the drawn reach to the measured proportion (V-SWEEP) and the crown-bottom-to-ring-top span to the field itself (V-LEN). Cable material RECORDED in the same chapter: anchor cables are split green bamboo strip, boiled then twisted (po xi qing mie) — hemp is the text’s sail and towing cordage, not the anchor’s. Drawn recovered, all five (r185): the bow-worked three on the foredeck, cables to the general's-posts and the barrel; the stern pair (shao yong er zhi — stations RECORDED) on the poop's top-tier roof, the surface MEASURED r185 (ray map, build/staging/r185): continuous u 0.68–1.00 at sheer + 4.18 m, ~11 m clear abeam at the stern stations, and already the drawn ship's aft working deck — the after-sheets are worked from it. The stern pair's weight is NOT RECORDED (qi yu — 'the rest'): the head pair's 300-catty inference at the forging text's own anvil threshold carries over, shank 2.0 m. The stern BELAY is in no text — the jiangjunzhu sentence names the bow posts — so each stern cable is drawn bent to its ring and flaked in a coil beside it, a stow, not an invented lead (the r182 grapnel standing). Stow spots PLACEMENT INFERENCE, measured and iterated (r182/r183 method). Member sections MASS-SOLVED r190: the r189 sections followed the plate's line weights and summed to 156 kg of wrought iron against the find's captioned 456 — a third of the record — so sections now come from the balance itself. The section RATIOS are a caliper record from the same harbour: the 2005 second dredge of the same basin raised a complete four-claw anchor, and the excavation brief (蓬莱3艘古船发掘简报 §7, haijiaoshi.com/archives/425, saved r190) measures it — shank 177 cm at ⌀8.5 cm, claws 73 cm at ⌀7 cm, one diameter over the claw's length, tips 144 cm apart, a head eye ⌀4.5, forge marks named on the surface. The absolute scale is solved per anchor so the drawn iron weighs the record's own mass at 7850 kg/m³ — the weight fields sheetKg 295 (RECORDED, the text's 500 catties), bowerKg/sternKg 177 (the standing 300-catty inference). At the calibrator, 456 kg draws shank ⌀15.5→11.9 cm and claw ⌀11.3→6.8 cm on 2.15 m; all three record anchors share one density class, so they solve to one proportion set and the r188 cube-law stands. The method checks itself against the calipers: the 2005 anchor's own members integrate to ~170 kg, and handing that mass and its ~1.94 m length back to the solve returns claw ⌀7.1 cm against the measured 7.0 and shank ⌀9.7 against 8.5. The claw centreline, crown ball and head eye stay the plate's (r189): a line drawing carries a silhouette, and only the sections were its line weights'. The audit holds each drawn anchor's integrated iron to its record's weight (V-MASS, 12%).

The Kiel Hansekogge's page (r235/hansekogge-an-bord.txt): 'Lediglich die Loecher im Ruestbalken, an denen die unteren Enden der Wanten befestigt sind, waren vorhanden.' The replicas (r236/ubena3-rail-band-2x.png, ubena2-rail-band-2x.png, roland-lower.png) set their shrouds up at the rail at the forward end of the castle's side wall, abaft the mast, as the plate has it. cog.hull.sectionProvenance: THE SHAPE, from the wreck's own section sheet. Lahn, Blatt 3 (r213/lahn-blatt2.jpg, a photographed plate at 640 px, about 30 px/m across the beam), Spant 26 mit Querbalken DB 4 — the fullest of the sheet's four sections and the nearest to midships (Spant 6 and 10 are V-sectioned at the bow, Spant 35 on the rising run aft) — read at 4x (r226/trace-spant26-4x.png), the outer face of the planking on both sides at eleven heights, averaged, as fractions of the RAIL'S half-breadth (113.75 plate px) and of the side's height keel plank to top strake (182.75 px): h/D 0.005 → 0.19, 0.022 → 0.35, 0.063 → 0.52, 0.145 → 0.65, 0.28 → 0.78, 0.42 → 0.90, 0.56 → 0.96, 0.69 → 0.99, 0.83 → 1.00, 1.0 → 1.00. Two facts the loft's superellipse could not draw: the side widens all the way to the top strake, so the BEAM IS AT THE RAIL (tumblehome 0, the 0.04 it replaces was a class default); and the bottom is a flat of flush-laid planks on the keel plank that the curve starts from. form 'flared': half-breadth B·(F + (1−F)·(1 − (1 − h/D)^n)^(1/n)), B the rail's. floorHalfFrac 0.15 and power 2.2 are a FIT to the ten read points (within 0.03 B at every height over 0.02 D; the superellipse to the waterline was 0.12 B too full at 0.28 D and 0.04 B too narrow at the rail). Fractions in each axis are the plate's own and do not depend on the photograph's aspect (the sheet reads D/B 0.80 where the record says 0.56, so the plate is not square and a 45° read off it would be wrong; the fractions are safe). Read precision ±2.5 plate px = ±0.02 B, ±0.014 D. FALLS OUT OF IT: the load waterline's half-breadth 0.92 B (7.0 m on a 7.6 m beam), the underwater section coefficient 0.78 (the record's cm 0.8 keeps its meaning as the old loft's coefficient; the wreck's own reads 0.77 by the same integration), and the turn of the bilge — the 45° tangent — 0.82 m over the keel where the superellipse put it at 1.05. Doel 1's carvel bottom (Vermeersch & Haneca 2014) is the class's other witness for the flat. ALONG THE SHIP (r227): the sheet's other three sections read the same way. r227/trace-sections.py seeds each section at its keel and walks the outer planking line upward (overlays r227/trace-spant5-4x.png, -spant12-, -spant33-, checked by eye: the trace holds the outer line to the rail on Spant 6, to about half the side's height on Spant 35 and 12 and wanders onto labels above that, so only the rows it holds are used; Spant 10's bottom rows sit on the Kielschwein label and were read by eye off r227/grid-spant12-4x.png instead). Rail half-breadths, plate px: Spant 6 104, Spant 10 115, Spant 26 114, Spant 35 113. Half-breadth as a fraction of each section's OWN rail half-breadth: Spant 6 at h/D 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.20 / 0.40 → 0.11 / 0.21 / 0.39 / 0.70; Spant 10 at 0.03 / 0.11 / 0.18 / 0.26 / 0.33 / 0.49 → 0.07 / 0.20 / 0.34 / 0.46 / 0.57 / 0.76; Spant 35 at 0.05 / 0.10 / 0.20 / 0.40 → 0.15 / 0.20 / 0.47 / 0.80; Spant 26 (r226) at 0.06 / 0.15 / 0.28 / 0.42 → 0.52 / 0.65 / 0.78 / 0.90. So the flat is midships only: at both ends the section is a V to the keel plank with no flat, and its curve is nearer a straight line than the midship's, while the rail is still 0.91–1.0 of the midship's — the flat is a property of the station, not of the breadth. stations[] carries the four as fits to the same family, floorHalfFrac and power per Spant (Spant 6 F 0 n 1.5, rms 0.05 B over h/D 0.02–0.8; Spant 10 F 0.0 n 1.4, rms 0.045 over the eye-read; Spant 35 F 0 n 1.6, rms 0.07 over 0.02–0.42; Spant 26 unchanged). The family cannot draw a straight V that rounds off above, which is what the end sections are: that is the residual, under 0.08 B. The loft interpolates F and n linearly in u between the stations and holds the end values beyond Spant 6 and 33; a station's u is its frame's (frameU, the inverse of frameNumber: 0.055 + 0.89·k/36 at the record's 0.5 m room and space — Spant 6 → 0.18, 12 → 0.35, 26 → 0.70, 33 → 0.87), which assumes the model's frame 0 is the wreck's Spant 0, ±1 frame. The numbering runs from the bow (Spant 35 carries the castle deck above its beam; r226). Read precision ±2.5 plate px = ±0.02 B. RAIL PLAN (r228): the same sheet's four rail half-breadths — 104 / 115 / 114 / 113 plate px at Spant 6 / 10 / 26 / 35 — as fractions of the widest (0.90 / 1.00 / 0.99 / 0.98, ±0.02 B) are each station's railHalfFrac, and the loft's plan is a monotone cubic through them from stemFineness at the stem to sternFineness at the post (railPlan). The class parabola (wlPower 2, stemFineness 0.2, sternFineness 0.24) read 0.67 / 0.93 / 0.88 / 0.58 at those stations — the stern a third of the beam too fine — and the three values stay in the record only as the plan's end values, because the sheet has no section forward of Spant 6 or abaft Spant 35, so the plan beyond the outermost stations is the loft's own, unread. The section forms above turn the rail plan into the waterline's, and the coefficients follow (r228/coeffs.py, the loft's underwater body integrated at the record's 2.25 m draught on the 20.5 m waterline): Cw 0.60 → 0.71, Cp 0.60 → 0.66, Cm 0.76 → 0.78, Cb 0.40 → 0.47, displacement 145 → 168 t (r231/coeffs.py, the r228 replica re-run on the stations where r230 put them, 0.146 / 0.234 / 0.657 / 0.847; the r228 numbers on the old stations were 0.59 → 0.70, 0.61 → 0.64, 0.76 → 0.78, 0.39 → 0.45 and 140 → 163 t - the held end forms and the rail plan now reach 0.5-1.0 m further toward each end, so the body fills). DERIVED, all five, and UNVERIFIED: the record holds no published displacement to check them against — the DSM booklet (r213/dsm-kogge-1380-booklet.pdf) gives the HOLD at about 160 m³, a cargo volume, not a displacement.
cog.hull.sternProvenance: Sharp-sterned on a straight raked post: the Bremen cog is double-ended, her planking closing on stem and sternpost (Lahn Blatt 9 elevation; the DSM booklet: 'vorn und achtern gerade Steven auf einer flachen Kielplanke'). transom 0 from r214 - the 0.3 it replaced drew a flat stern face above water that no plate supports. The castle's stern beams overhang the post; the hull does not. THE POST'S LINE is on the record from r237 (hull.sternpost): straight, 110 deg to the keel, through the waterline's after end, from the keel's underside to a head 5.05 m over it; the loft's stern profile IS that line at every height, under the water as well as over it, where before r237 the skin ended in a vertical cut at the waterline's after end and the post ran buried inside the after body from u 0.90 at the keel to u 1.0 at the sheer. THE HOOD ENDS (r238): the planking closes on the post's rabbet (hull.sternpost.hoodEndHalfBreadthM), not on a flat end cap; the rail plan's after end is that half-breadth where before it was the class's sternFineness.
cog.hull.framesProvenance: THAT THEY STAND THERE: the wreck's own timbers. The Bremen cog is framed with floor timbers (Bodenwrangen) and futtocks (Auflanger) put in after the shell was planked, and the futtocks' upper ends stand against the inside of the planking above the deck, between the beam knees, up to the top strake: the DSM's photograph of the hull from above (r213/wreck-in-bremerhaven.jpg, no scale) shows them against the starboard planking under and beside the deck, and Lahn's Blatt 3 titles each section by its Spant number. PITCH, a CLASS DEFAULT: 0.50 m room-and-space is not a fetched number. Lahn 1992 draws the frames on Blaetter 3, 7, 8, 24 and 28-34 (the book's contents list via modellmarine.de, r217) and none of those sheets has been fetched; the Blatt 3 section titles do not resolve their Spant numbers at 640 px (r215). Bounds: the Poel cog of 1354 carried 50 frames (Mittelalter-Lexikon, 'Kogge'), about 0.4 m of pitch on a hull of that length; the DSM photograph reads roughly a futtock's siding of gap between futtocks. A 35-40 cm figure a search returned (Mitteilungen der DGAMN) describes a scrapped wreck whose frames had been taken out and is NOT this ship. Precision +-0.15 m. SIDING 0.18 m and MOULDING 0.20 m are class defaults below what any plate here resolves. Built (r217): one frame every room-and-space over the same run the class-default frames use, from the keel to a hand under the rail cap, the outer face 5 cm inside the skin; no frame within a timber's siding of a through-beam, where the standing knee is the timber against the skin. The Shipwright shows them in the planked stages on this hull because the record says the deck lies below the sheer (deck.belowSheerM); on every other hull the frames stay hidden once the planking is on. THE HEAD (r223): read off the DSM's plate of the hull from over the bow (r213/wreck-dsm-side.jpg, 3840 x 2543, the port side forward, crop r223/crop-port-heads-grid.png). The plate has no scale bar, so its scale comes from the futtock siding itself, about 45 px to a siding, which is 250 px/m if the siding is 0.18 m and 200 px/m if it is 0.22; every number below is a RATIO to the siding and is only as good as that class default. Nine futtock heads in the crop: each narrows toward the head, the topmost 0.3 m reading 40 px against 50-55 px at the deck, so headSidedFrac 0.78 (+-0.08), the narrowing spread over about the top 1.2 m (headTaperM, +-0.4). Every head is rounded off, no square cut among the nine (headRound). The heads stand at the top strake's upper edge or a hand under it (0-16 cm, +-5 cm), which is where r217 already put them; two forward heads stand proud of the planking because the strake there is broken away, not because the head was higher. THE SAME CROP ON THE PITCH: heads stand 75-82 px apart centre to centre against a 40-50 px siding, a room-and-space of 1.8 (+-0.2) sidings, which is 0.32-0.36 m at siding 0.18 and 0.40-0.44 m at 0.22; this is scale-free and tightens the class default's 0.35-0.65 bound to its lower half, but the pitch is NOT changed until a plate resolves the siding in metres. NOT BUILT (r223, named residual): the plate shows the floors' arm heads standing beside the futtocks at about mid-side, rounded like the heads above, the two timbers lying side by side and lapped, not scarfed end to end; the model's frame is one timber from the keel to the head. The moulding at the head is unread: this plate looks at the futtocks' inner faces. THE LAP (r224): the frame is not one timber. The same plate (r213/wreck-dsm-side.jpg, the port side forward; crops r224/crop-port-heads-2x-left.png and crop-port-lap-3x.png) shows, beside every futtock that reaches the rail, a SECOND timber whose rounded head stands under the futtock's head by 110-135 px in the plate's vertical, which the plate compresses because it looks down the side; read against the strakes, whose seams lie 75-85 px apart in the same crop and which are 0.4-0.6 m wide, that is about a strake and a half, 0.75 m (+-0.25): laps[0].headBelowM. In the three pairs the 3x crop resolves, the lower timber stands FORWARD of the futtock and touches it, so the model stands it one siding forward. The feet of both timbers are hidden by the forward beam and the modern shoring (crop-port-lower-2x.png), so the LAP LENGTH is not read from this plate: lapM 1.0 is a class value with bounds 0.5-2.0 taken from Doel 1, a cog of the same century (Vermeersch & Haneca, IJNA 2014; r224/doel1.txt): its second set of futtocks ends between strakes GN and GP and the third runs from GN or GP to the sheer-strake, a lap of nought to two strakes; its futtocks are 1.40-3.41 m long, c. 0.20 m sided and 0.14 m moulded, its floors 0.22 sided and 0.14 moulded, with up to three futtocks a side over the floor. The lower head is built tapered and rounded like the top one because the plate shows it rounded (Doel 1's uppermost futtocks were cut horizontally, which the Bremen plate does not bear out); its taper is not read separately. What the plate shows and the record does not yet carry: the floors are single timbers over the bottom (r223/crop-side-stbd-mid.png) and lap the futtocks at the turn of the bilge, a second lap with no number here; Doel 1 sets that scarf alternately below and above the bilge. THE FLOOR'S LAP (r225), a CLASS VALUE, not a read: no plate here shows it. r223/crop-side-stbd-mid.png, which r223 and r224 read as floors lying over the bottom with a second timber beside each at the bilge, shows STRAKES: the parallel timbers run with the ship and each carries a row of treenail heads spaced 35 px, one per frame, the rows lying across them (r225/crop-stbd-bilge-1.6x.png), so that crop cannot give a floor's head; Lahn's Blatt 3 sections (r213/lahn-blatt2.jpg, 640 px) do not resolve a lap; the DSM booklet and Westphal 1991 carry no section. Doel 1 (Vermeersch & Haneca, IJNA 2014, r224/doel1.txt) gives the class: 'the floor timbers end either on strake GC or GF', each floor with 'one bilge scarf alternating to port and starboard', 'the scarfs between the floor timbers and the first futtocks are set alternately below or above the bilge (strakes GB/GC or GE/GF)'. GC is the last strake of Doel 1's carvel bottom, so the SHORT arm ends at the turn of the bilge and the LONG arm three strakes higher, 0.9 m at Doel 1's ~0.3 m strakes (altM, +-0.3). headAboveKeelM 1.1 is the MODEL'S OWN bilge: the height over the keel at which the lofted section's tangent passes 45 degrees at u 0.47 (y -1.16 over a keel at -2.25); the wreck's section is flatter over the bottom and harder at the turn than the loft (Lahn Blatt 3), so its bilge may stand lower, +-0.3 m. lapM 1.0 is the top lap's class value (0.5-2.0). Which side is long on which frame is recorded for no cog: the model puts the long arm to port on the even frames. Doel 1 says the Bremen cog has six strakes fewer than its eighteen, twelve; the loft's strakes field says 14 and is not from this source. R226: headAboveKeelM 0.8 replaces 1.1 — the value is the model's own turn of the bilge (the 45° tangent of the section at u 0.47), and the section is now the plate's (hull.section, Blatt 3 Spant 26), whose bilge turns at 0.82 m over the keel; the superellipse's turned at 1.05–1.09. altM 0.9 and lapM 1.0 unchanged (class values, Doel 1). And the floor's own lap (laps[1].lapM) is 0.6, not the top lap's 1.0: the floor's short arm ends 0.8 m over the keel, and a futtock lapped a metre down beside it would have its foot under the keel — the builder clamps a foot at the keel and the audit convicted all 33 frames ('a lap off its length', 0.77 m of 1.0, r226/audit-first.out) on the section's first run. Doel 1 (Vermeersch & Haneca 2014) gives the floor-to-futtock scarf as nought to two strakes, 0–0.6 m at its 0.3 m strakes; the class takes the upper bound, so the middle futtock's foot stands 0.2 m over the keel beside the short arm and 1.1 m beside the long one. ORIGIN (r230): frames.originU -0.019 is the u of Spant 0 of Lahn's numbering, the origin frameU and frameNumber count from. Fitted from Blatt 1's four named heads (u 0.146 / 0.234 / 0.657 / 0.847 through the built hull, see deck.provenance) against Tanner 2021's frame numbers 6 / 10 / 26 / 35 at the class pitch 0.89/36 u (0.507 m): the four give -0.002 / -0.013 / +0.014 / -0.018, median -0.008, the spread being the ship's own uneven framing (0.1-0.4 m). The origin therefore lies between two and three frames forward of the run's first frame; -0.019 (three frames: frame f of the run is Spant f+3) is taken, the nearer of the two values at which the numbered stations coincide with the built run's frames, so a beam still displaces the frame at its station; +0.006 (two frames) is the other, and a fetch of Lahn's Blatt 35 body plan with its frame numbers would choose between them. Spant 0 therefore stands 0.4 m FORWARD of the waterline's forward end, at the stem, and the run's first frame (u 0.055) is Spant 3; before r230 the run's first frame was taken for Spant 0 and every numbered station sat about 1.5 m too far aft. The numbers rise aft (Tanner 2021, Appendix H). The floor's long arm changes side by Spant number, so the parity the model draws moved with the origin; no source gives it. SHEET NUMBER (r230): the photographed section sheet r213/lahn-blatt2.jpg is Lahn's Blatt 3, not Blatt 2 as modellmarine.de's filename has it: Tanner cites 'Blatt 3: Spant 35 mit Querbalken DB 5' and 'frames 6, 10, 26 and 35 on Blatt 3', which is this sheet's content, and its own title block does not resolve at 640 px; the numbers this record carries are Tanner's read, not the photograph's.
cog.hull.windlassProvenance: The wreck's own machine. The reconstructed Bremen cog carries a windlass athwartships UNDER THE AFTCASTLE DECK, forward of the helmsman — Ellmers (DSM, Drassana): 'the man at the tiller had to stand ... behind the heavy windlass' — with a separate capstan (Gangspill) on the castle top, NOT drawn (residual r173). Dimensions are the Kiel replica's build record to the DSM's own Lahn plans: Bratspill 4.5 m long, 60 cm thick (Baykowski 1991, via de.wikipedia Bremer Kogge — TEXT reads, no plate scale applies). Station u 0.875 is Ellmers's 'in its middle' applied to the castle's RECORDED run (r214: the plan's 8.2 m from u 0.70 to the after edge at 1.02, so its middle is x 8.1 m abaft midships, u 0.875 by the loft); before r214 it was a text read of 0.82 against a guessed run. Precision is the overhang read's, ±0.02 u. Barrel underside 0.30 m over the deck, the eight-square barrel, two standards and two shipped handspikes are CLASS DEFAULTS from Falconer 1769 WINDLASS ('holes bored through the body', 'lower part ... about a foot above the deck'), named cross-tradition. The aftcastle over the machine is drawn as of r205 (see castleProvenance); the barrel keeps its attested place beneath the castle deck. Whether the ORIGINAL barrel was among the >2,000 recovered pieces is not established by the sources fetched in r173; the claim is the reconstruction and the replicas, not the find inventory. The Gangspill on the castle top is drawn from r212 (see capstanProvenance).

The loft places the wing's forward end and the step at stationsU (u = 0.5 + (8.39 - d) / 20.5, the r230 conversion; the after edge stays at castle.overhangAftM abaft the built post's head, the r214 rule). THE AFTER EDGE (r237): the castle's after wall's outer face stands at plate x 331 at the castle deck (y 1300, 5.31 m over the keel) and x 278 at the rail (y 580, 6.53 m): 3.10 m abaft the datum at the deck, 3.19 at the rail (r237/blatt1-stern-upper-full.png; the row scans in the r237 handoff). stationsFromHeelM.aftEdge -3.10 (negative: abaft the datum) is where the loft now puts the after edge, through the datum the straight post gives it (hull.sternpost.footAbaftStationDatumM); overhangAftM becomes a DERIVED number, 0.15: the post's head (5.05 m over the keel, after face at x 426, 2.93 m abaft the datum) to the after edge. Before r237 the after edge stood 4.0 m abaft the datum, chained 0.7 m abaft a post whose head was 0.7 m too far aft (the bent, over-raked class post); the Blatt 9 read of 0.7 at 60 px/m is superseded by Blatt 1 at 590.8.
cog.hull.castleProvenance: The wreck's own structure, and from r214 its own PLAN. The Bremen cog's aftcastle is preserved to its highest rail and stands whole on the reconstructed ship; Ellmers (Drassana, r173): 'a windlass in its middle and a capstan on its top', the man at the tiller 'underneath the castle-deck in between the long cabins at both sides and behind the heavy windlass'. PLAN, RECORD numbers (Westphal, DAS LOGBUCH 27/1991 H.4 p.128, the Kiel replica's build report citing Lahn, Das Achterkastell der Hansekogge, Deutsche Schiffahrt 1/1979): an after part trapezoidal in plan, 4.75 m long, 7.20 m broad at its forward edge and 6.50 m at its after edge, plus two side parts each 3.45 m long and 1.65 m broad; the castle deck cross-planked over fore-and-aft beams, those on athwartship beams on vertical posts; the castle overhangs the main deck aft and at both sides, so the after posts stand on two stern beams (Heckbalken), the forward of which is propped amidships; the starboard side wall's lower part three stringer-like timbers and a plank, its upper part 17 vertical boards (counted from nail traces, three boards found). Before 1978 the reconstruction assumed a simple open platform; the wall fragments overturned that, which is why the r205 open parapet is replaced by walls. PLATE READ, Lahn Blatt 9 elevation at 60 px/m (Tanner & Belasus 2021 fig. 1, r213): the castle's after edge stands about 0.5 m abaft the sternpost's after face at the castle deck's height (±0.2 m), which is 0.7 m abaft the post's after face where it meets the top strake, the post raking about 0.4 m per metre of height there — overhangAftM 0.7 is measured from the strake, where the stern beams lie, the castle deck is level, and the whole 8.2 m reads as one deck line — so the side parts are wings at the castle deck's own level along each side, the main deck open between them; the Roland von Bremen replica photographed from the quarter (r213/roland-ubena.jpg) shows exactly that: vertical-boarded walls on beam ends overhanging stern and sides, narrow decked wings forward with lower walls. PHOTOGRAPH READS, no scale: the wing walls stand about 0.6 of the after part's wall; the after end is walled like the sides. CLASS DEFAULTS, named: 1.95 m from afterdeck to castle deck at the helmsman's station (the castle deck is set level there); the parapet 1.0 m; beams sided ~0.2 m, the Heckbalken 0.26; the lower wall 0.6 m deep; open rails on the wings' inner edges and forward ends and the breastrail over the open deck (no wall is recorded there); the two long cabins under the after part. fromU/toU are now DERIVED from the plan (the forward end at u 0.70, the after edge at 1.03, past the post) and kept in the record only for the builders that read them. The DSM booklet gives the ship as 7.02 m high to the winch on the castle deck; Lahn's elevation reads the castle deck about 5.4 m over the keel's underside. This model's castle deck stands about a metre higher over the water than that, because the model lays the cog's main deck at the sheer where the real deck lies a bulwark's height below it — a residual named in r214, not a castle fault. Lahn 1992 (Schriften des DSM 30) carries the castle sheets themselves — NOT fetched; a fetched plate would supersede the reads above. No forecastle: the wreck has none (Westphal, note 2), and none is drawn. HEIGHT (r232): the castle deck stands at Tanner 2021's 5.34 m over the keel's underside (Appendix H, 5260 mm at Frame 26 and 5343 at Frame 35; castle.deckAboveKeelM), on the same datum as the deck's beams (deck.beamHeightsFromKeelM), and it was HELD there while the main deck under it dropped to its read height, so the headroom over the afterdeck at the helmsman's station is derived by the loft (about 2.5 m; the class default deckHM 1.95 is retired from this record) and everything under the castle - the windlass, the cabins, the tiller at the helmsman's hand - reads the deck it stands on.
cog.hull.capstanProvenance: The wreck's own capstan. The Gangspill was recovered WITH the Bremen cog from the Weser in the 1960s and is in the Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum's collection, Inv. I/11066/14 (museum-digital:bremen, object 3): oak, D 56 cm, H 176 cm — both RECORD numbers, the museum's own measurements of the recovered timber. The form is the museum's description: the rope ran round the lower wooden cone ('Das Windentau lief um den unteren Holzkegel') and the handspikes shipped into rectangular holes through the body above it; the museum says it was used to work the square sail round to the wind. Position: Ellmers (DSM, Drassana) — the aftcastle carries 'a windlass in its middle and a capstan on its top' — so it stands on the castle deck; atU 0.875 is 'its middle' applied to the castle's recorded plan (r214, see castleProvenance), ±0.02 u; Lahn's Blatt 9 elevation draws the Gangspill nearer the castle's forward end, about 1 m abaft it — a plate read at 60 px/m that contradicts the text by some 3 m, left with the text because the elevation cannot say which side of the centreline the machine stands on and the forward 3.45 m of the castle is two wings with open deck between. The head/cone split (head a little over half the height), the cone's neck (about 40 cm under the shoulder) and the head's breadth (a squared eight-sided block wider than the neck) are READS off the museum's oblique photograph, which carries no scale; the two through-shipped handspikes and the step under the foot are class defaults — the record does not give the count of holes. The Kiel replica's build record (Baykowski 1991) lists the Gangspill finished beside the Bratspill in 1987.
cog.hull.rudderProvenance: The wreck's own irons. One of two RUDERÖSEN (rudder gudgeons) recovered with the Bremen cog is in the Deutsches Schiffahrtsmuseum, Inv. I/10393/08 (museum-digital:bremen object 22): iron, L×B×H 35 × 30 × 13 cm, a short tube with a massive clamp forged to it whose rectangular plates clasp the sternpost; the museum's text says four were needed to hang the rudder and that the blade must have carried downward pintles to drop into them — so hangings 4 is a RECORD number, and the pintle-on-blade, gudgeon-on-post arrangement is the record's. Ellmers (DSM, Drassana, r173): the two upper gudgeons were never nailed on, so the cog sank unfinished with her rudder not yet hung — the blade itself is NOT among the finds. The blade's form is Lahn's reconstruction, Blatt 9 elevation at 1:20 (reproduced as Tanner & Belasus 2021 fig. 1, Archaeonautica 21, CC BY, fetched r213 at 60 px/m): a narrow blade parallel to the raked sternpost from the post's heel to the castle's after beam, four hangings ticked along it, the tiller level forward under the castle deck. Chords are READS off that plate at 60 px/m: 0.60 m at the foot, 0.45 m at the head, ±0.15 m — the plate cannot support better. Tiller station u 0.90 is a TEXT read of Ellmers (the man at the tiller stood behind the windlass, which is at u 0.875 since r214), ±0.04 u; its height is the castle deck's underside less the beam and a hand's clearance, a class default. Stock siding (three quarters of the post's), the number and taper of the back pieces, strap breadth and the pintle knuckle's size are class defaults named in buildTimberRudder; the clamp plate's 35 cm on the post is the recovered iron's own length. Lahn 1992 (Die Kogge von Bremen, Schriften des DSM 30) carries an 'Achtersteven' sheet — NOT fetched; its numbers would supersede every read here.
cog.hull.deck.provenance: COVERING: a planked deck, from the record — Westphal (DAS LOGBUCH 27/1991 H.4 p.128): 'Ebenso wie das Hauptdeck ist auch das Kasteldeck über Längsbalken querbeplankt' — the main deck is planked ATHWARTSHIPS over fore-and-aft beams; plankRun 'athwart' lays the model's planks that way (r216; the seams run across the ship, the butts along it). The plank width and butt length are class defaults. DEPTH, READ (r231): the deck lies BELOW the top strake, on through-beams, and Lahn's Blatt 1 at 590.8 px/m (r230/lahn-blatt1-full.png; the columns rail-to-keel at each head, r231/col-DB1..DB5.png) says how far. Each head's centre stands 3.42 / 2.23 / 2.01 / 2.04 / 2.31 m over the keel's underside amidships (plate y 4442, the datum Tanner's Table 6 heights close on to the pixel: 4273 mm at midships; deck.beamHeightsFromKeelM, +-0.10) and 1.10 / 2.23 / 2.26 / 2.28 / 1.97 m under the washboard's top at the same x (deck.railAboveBeamCentreM, +-0.10). The Blatt 3 sections at Spant 10 and Spant 26 (r231/sec-spant10-db2.png, sec-spant26-db4.png, from the 640 px photograph) agree to 0.2 m once the through-beam's own band is told from the carlings standing on it, and they put the deck's surface - the carlings' tops, the planking on those - about 0.5 m over the beam's centre (deck.deckAboveBeamCentreM, +-0.15). So the main deck stands 2.5-2.8 m over the keel and 1.75 m under the rail at DB 2-4, 1.47 m at DB 5. DB 1 is a level higher: its head is 1.2 m above DB 2's and 1.10 m under the rail, a platform at the bow, and both Kiel replicas photographed (r213/ubena-kiel2007-2.jpg, r231/ubena-bow-3x.png: a person at the stem seen from the waist up; r213/roland-ubena.jpg, r231/roland-bow-2x.png: a decked platform with a cross-timber at the bow above the waist's deck) carry one, unmeasured. Two earlier reads are voided by this one: 'a third of the side under the sheer' (r215, 1.3-1.4 m) took the carlings' tops at Spant 10 for the beam, and the Blatt 9 chain (0.8-1.1 m) ran through a class-default castle headroom of 1.95 m where the castle deck stands 3.0 m over DB 5's centre (Tanner's Table 6: 5260 mm at Frame 26, 5343 at Frame 35). BUILT (r232): the deck now lies ON the beams at these heights, the loft's deck line a monotone cubic through them - belowSheerContest has the arithmetic and what stays contested; belowSheerM 1.75 is the plate's midship number (4.27 - 2.51), the one the audit's D-DEPTH reads, and level is false. LEVEL: the heads from DB 2 aft rise 0.22 m at DB 2 and 0.30 m at DB 5 over DB 3-4, a sheer of the deck's own, gentler than the rail's; DB 1 stands a level higher. throughBeams 5 is the sheet's own numbering (DB 1 to DB 5) — a floor, not a census; STATIONS (r230, replacing r229's): the five heads are READ off Lahn's Blatt 1, the starboard elevation at 1:20 (Google Arts & Culture, DSM asset ngGyF3o9Vjp9CA, fetched whole by tiles at 14338 x 4699 px, 590.8 px/m by its own 2500 mm bar, r230/lahn-blatt1-full.png), where each through-beam's end is drawn as a cross-hatched square about 0.45 m on a side with its wedge beneath; measured forward of the sternpost's aft face at the keel (plate x 2160, +-0.1 m): DB 1 15.82, DB 2 13.91, DB 3 8.68, DB 4 5.18, DB 5 1.16 m (deck.beamHeadsFromHeelM, +-0.15). Carried as each station's u DERIVED THROUGH THE BUILT HULL: the model's heel is the sternpost's aftmost foot vertex, x 8.39 (the audit's datum, D-BEAM-HEEL), and a beam placed at u lands on the raked skin at x = (u - 0.5)*lwl shifted by -0.34 m at DB 1 at the foredeck's height (r232; -0.18 at the r230 deck height), -0.06 at DB 2, 0 amidships and +0.11 at DB 5 (r230/audit-first.out against the record), so the u's that put the built heads at the sheet's distances are 0.154 / 0.234 / 0.486 / 0.657 / 0.847 (DB 1's re-derived in r232: at the foredeck's height the head exits the raked bow 0.16 m further forward than at the old deck height, so its u moved aft by 0.008; 0.146 before); the spant is the sheet's label. Read against the heel without the loft (8.39 - d, no shift) they would be 0.138 / 0.231 / 0.486 / 0.657 / 0.853. The section sheet's frame numbers are Tanner 2021's read of the physical sheet (Southampton thesis, Appendix H, r230/tanner-vol2.txt: 'frames 6, 10, 26 and 35 on Blatt 3', 'Blatt 3: Spant 35 mit Querbalken DB 5'): 6 / 10 / 26 / 35, not r226's 5 / 12 / 26 / 33 off a 640 px photograph whose titles do not resolve (r230/sec-titles-stacked.png). DB 3 has no section; its head is on Blatt 1 and its number, 20 (+-1), follows from the origin. The numbering runs from the BOW aft (Tanner: 'from frame 19 aft to frame 28', the castle wall 'to frame 36', DB 5 carrying the windlass under the castle); Spant 0 is at frames.originU. Blatt 1's own bottom scale, 'Rekonstruktionsspant-Nr.' 0-18, is a DIFFERENT numbering: metre stations from the stern (0 at 0.35 m forward of the heel, 18 at the stem's foot, 589 px = 1.0 m apart), not the frames. HEIGHT: built r232 on the beams' read heights (DEPTH above, and belowSheerContest). DATUM (r237): the 'sternpost's heel' these distances are measured from, plate x 2160, is the keel plank's after end at the stern hook's lower scarf, 1.12 m forward of the post's own foot (hull.sternpost.footAbaftStationDatumM); the distances stand as read.
cog.hull.sternpost.provenance: THE LINE (r237). Lahn's Blatt 1 (r230/lahn-blatt1-full.png, 590.8 px/m; crops r237/blatt1-heel-full.png, blatt1-stern-post-half.png, blatt1-stern-upper-full.png) draws the sternpost's after face as ONE straight line from the keel's underside to the stern beams: read by row scan every 100 px from plate y 4440 (the keel's underside) to y 1640, the leftmost line inside the border stands at x 1499 at the keel and x 492 at 4.74 m over it, 1007 px aft over 2800 px up, 0.3596 m aft per metre of height, an angle of 109.8 deg to the keel, carried as 110. CORRECTED r238: the two Tanner passages r237 quoted for the angle are OTHER VESSELS' - 'a stern post at the determined 110 deg angle (taken from archaeological and historical parallels)' is the Newport ship's reconstruction (vol. 2 App. G, r230/tanner-vol2.txt line 7805, under the App. G header at 7780), and 'the missing sternpost extended in a straight line continuing from the top of the sternhook' is the Drogheda boat's (App. F, lines 4760-4766, header at 4740). The cog's angle rests on the plate alone; Tanner's 110 is a parallel from the same author's other reconstruction. The line's residual from straight over 2800 px is under 3 px. THE HEAD: the line ends between 5.01 and 5.11 m over the keel (rows 1480 and 1420), under the stern beams whose hatched ends stand 5.11-5.3 m; headAboveKeelM 5.05 +-0.05. THE FOOT AND THE DATUM: the after face meets the keel's underside at plate x 1499. r230 named plate x 2160 'the sternpost's aft face at the keel' and measured every station on this record from it (deck.beamHeadsFromHeelM, castle.stationsFromHeelM, mast.shroudFixing.stationsFromHeelM); x 2160 is the keel plank's after end at the stern hook's lower scarf (the flat bottom steps 40 px, 7 cm, between x 2055 and 2180: r237/blatt1-heel-full.png, r230/datum-sternheel.png), 661 px = 1.12 m forward of the post's foot. Every 'FromHeelM' number stays as read against x 2160; footAbaftStationDatumM carries the correction, and the loft and the audit place the datum 1.12 m forward of the built post's foot. THE WATERLINE'S AFTER END: at 2.25 m over the keel the after face stands at x 1021, 1.93 m abaft the datum, which is the model's lwl/2 (10.25 m abaft midships) to 4 cm - the record's lwl 20.5 and the post's line agree, so the loft runs the line through the waterline's after end at the record's draught. THE KEEL: flat. The keel's underside line lies at plate y 4441-4447 at x 2843 (DB 5), 3500, 5000 and 7290, and the hook's bottom at 4445-4452 at x 1700-2000: no rise toward the post; riseA 0.02 (was 0.28, the class's swept run, which lifted the model's keel 0.63 m at the post). hull.sternRake 0.09 stays on the record for the stem's clamp (rakeScale, r129) and is not read for a straight post. NOT READ: the post's moulded and sided dimensions (the plate draws a second line 0.27-0.30 m forward of the after face at 1.76, 2.25 and 2.78 m, the forward face or the rabbet; the class draws 0.225 m moulded and 0.42 sided); the stern hook itself as a timber (Lahn 1992 is not on disk; r237 cited Tanner's Figure 8 and 'grown timbers for the stem and stern hook', line 6260, for it, and both are the Drogheda boat's - Figure 8 is J. Ryan's drawing under the App. F header at 4206, line 6260 stands under the same header; corrected r239); the curve of the top strakes' hood ends up to the head.
cog.hull.sternpost.hoodEndProvenance: THE HOOD ENDS (r238). The strakes end ON the post: Lahn's Blatt 1 draws every strake line running into the sternpost's forward line from the keel to the top strake (r237/blatt1-stern-post-half.png, 590.8 px/m), and Tanner 2021 App. H Figure 14 (Lahn's Blatt 35 body plan lofted, r238/tanner-contact.png) shows the after body closing to the post with no end face. A clinker plank's hood end sits in the post's rabbet, so the skin's half-breadth where it meets the post is the post's half-siding less the rabbet's depth: 0.21 m (the class siding, 5.5% of beam = 0.42 m; Lahn's own siding is NOT on disk) less 0.04, DERIVED, not read. Before r238 the plan closed to sternFineness 0.24 (0.91 m half-breadth, a flat end cap 0.7 m wide each side of a 0.42 m post) because the class end value stood where the sheet has no station. NOT READ: the closing of the rail plan over the last 3.5 m from Spant 35 (0.98 of the beam) to the post; the sheet's stations stop at 35, and Blatt 35's body plan as Tanner reproduces it (125 px/m) carries no station spacing to place its after sections along the hull. The loft closes it with the monotone cubic's own end tangent (railPlan): 3.0 m half-breadth 2 m before the post, 1.55 m at 1 m.
cog.hull.stem.provenance: THE LINE (r239). Lahn's Blatt 1 (r230/lahn-blatt1-full.png, 590.8 px/m; crops r239/blatt1-bow-quarter.png, blatt1-stem-lower-half.png, blatt1-stem-foot-full.png, blatt1-stem-head-full.png) draws the stem's forward face as ONE straight line from the keel plank to a head far over the rail: read by row scan every 100 px from plate y 4420 (0.03 m over the keel's underside at y 4440) to y 260, the rightmost line inside the border (the title block excluded below y 3400) stands at x 11246 at the keel and x 14087 at 7.08 m over it, 2841 px forward over 4160 px up. A least-squares line through 46 rows: 0.6794 m forward per metre of height, 124.19 deg to the keel, no row more than 20 px (3.5 cm) off it, rms 6 px; the slope runs 0.700 in the lowest metre and 0.670 in the top two, a convexity of 3 cm over 7 m that the record carries as straight. THE FOOT: the forward face runs straight down to the flat bottom and meets it at plate x 11250-11256, y 4435, where the plate draws its own reference cross (blatt1-stem-foot-full.png): 15.40 m forward of the station datum at x 2160 (the keel plank's after end, hull.sternpost.footAbaftStationDatumM). THE HEAD: the forward face ends at y 260 (7.08 m over the keel) and the after face at y 180 (7.21 m), the top cut square to the timber; headAboveKeelM 7.1 +-0.1. The after face runs 230-240 px (0.39-0.41 m horizontal) behind the forward face over the top three metres and the timber is drawn broader at the hook. A block 0.1 m proud of the forward face at 6.6-6.75 m (x 13932-13998, y 460-540) is a fitting at the head, not the line. THE KEEL: flat to the hook. The keel's underside lies at plate y 4437-4451 from x 10400 to 11250 (14.0-15.4 m forward of the datum) against y 4441-4447 amidships: no rise toward the stem; riseF 0.02 (was 0.3, the class's cut-away forefoot, which lifted the model's keel 0.68 m at the bow). WHERE THE LINE CROSSES THE WATER: at 2.25 m over the keel (the record's laden draught) the forward face stands at x 12156, 16.92 m forward of the datum; the post's after face stands 1.93 m abaft it (r237), so the plate's length on that waterline is 18.85 m. hull.stemRake 0.1 stays on the record for the class clamp (rakeScale, r129) and is not read for a straight stem. NOT READ: the stem hook as a timber (its scarf to the keel plank and the bolted lap across it, blatt1-stem-foot-full.png); the stem's moulded and sided dimensions (Lahn 1992 is not on disk); the fitting at the head and the spar drawn against the head above the rail (Lahn's bowline spar).

The FORM is the tradition's, a NAVY-TRADITION EXTENSION stated here: the West Sea composite of oak shank (닻채), hook-arms hung both sides (닻가지), and a long grooved rectangular anchor-stone (닻돌) lashed on, because oak alone will not sink — the stone serving as the stock, 석제 닻장 in the report's own words. The type is RECORDED on her own coast: 154 anchor stones off Taean and Incheon, 2008–2019, rope grooves cut for the lashing, the wooden anchors found with them radiocarbon-dated from the 2nd century BC through Joseon — her own dynasty inside the run (Korea Heritage Service 2021). The band's ceiling runs to 590 kg, so larger stones are attested in the corpus; none fetched carries its own catalogue entry above 458, and that gap is stated. At 458 kg the stone is a load the drawn four-man horong breaks out at its bars' purchase. The ARMS take the form study's own count and splay (r196): TWO — every stock-anchor Hong 2013 draws carries two (그림 16 forms A–D, the stone-stock schematic 그림 17, and all six artifact reconstructions on p.135), and the institute's reconstruction figure draws two limbs at staggered whipped stations. The cable-hung stone the thesis keeps as a plausible AUXILIARY for strong current, a second small stone bent to the cable — named here, not drawn. CONTESTED, the report's own sentence: no stone has been confirmed still lashed to its shank (닻돌이 닻채에 묶인 상태로 확인된 사례가 없어 추측만) — the station is the record's reconstruction, not a find; the boatwright's Chinese cognate (마광남, 배목수이야기 42) stands beside it. The one stone recovered still JOINTED to its timber (마도해역-212, raised articulated 2014, 2017 시굴보고서) is the Chinese two-shank INSERT form, pegged through mortised battens — a different joint, so the Korean lashed form's sentence stands (r199) — and that insert form is now attested aboard a Korean-built Goryeo coaster (송호리1호선, Haenam, hull dated AD 1021–1158, excavation report 2025: one oak half, 149.5 cm printed, stowed inside the hull), so the form crossed hull traditions without touching the lashed form's own evidence. Stow is PLACEMENT INFERENCE, the fleet rule: under way the anchor lies recovered on the open foredeck beside its own horong, rolled so no member stands upright, the cable bent at the head and led to the barrel. The boatwright's trip-ring and buoy are a fishing practice with no warship warrant — not drawn. No fetched source draws a 16th-century warship's anchor directly; the album is two centuries after her and the gap is stated. One more drawn witness in her own line since r206: the 문헌편's plates chapter (국립해양유산연구소, 학술총서 91집, pdf p. 143) reproduces the 귀선도 — two ink drawings of the roofed ship, 개인 소장 (최순선), on deposit with the 국가유산청 현충사관리소, undated in its caption — and both hang an anchor from the hull's end on a steeply angled shank with two curved arms crossing at the crown. In the two-masted drawing that end is unambiguously the BOW, beside the dragon head — the placement the drawn machine follows, against the encyclopedia's stern-drum variant named above; the roofed side view hangs the same form below its arched end-housing, and which end that housing caps is not resolved. The reproduction bounds the read: the ship spans about 1,500 px on the 300-dpi page — roughly 50 px/m if she is near the 도설's scale — and the anchor about 200 px, so the two-armed crossed form and the bow station are legible and nothing finer: no stone, no lashing, no stock can be affirmed or denied at that scale.

The machine is attested three ways in her line. Her navy's own album, the Gakseondobon (c. 1797), carries it on the grain-ship plate: the National Maritime Heritage Institute's 2011 reconstruction of that plate (24 m) sets the horong at the bow, and the launch record says the horong was recreated from the drawing. The institute's component classification of the excavated Goryeo ships lists the horong among the anchoring gear (정박구: 닻, 호롱, 닻돌, 엄말) — read in the institute's site excerpts; the carrying page was not pinned, and no claim is made that a wreck preserved a horong timber. The living tradition gives the machine's working: a drum with two long bars passed through at different points, crossed, four men at the ends, about one coil of cable wound on (옛 돛단배의 언어 3). The album's warship plate draws the anchor; whether it also draws the windlass is NOT established by the sources fetched. CONTESTED placement: the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture's hanseon description fixes an anchor-winding drum at the STERN board beside the rudder; the drawn machine follows the naval line's build record, at the bow.
